title: MB4-04520
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the principal appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their minor daughter, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their minor son, who are all Venezuelan citizens, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the principal appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their minor daughter, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their minor son, who are all Venezuelan citizens, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). They maintain that the RPD unreasonably undermined their credibility and erred in its interpretation of the facts. They also maintain that there were a number of problems at the RPD hearing that adversely affected their claims for refugee protection.

The principal appellant was previously named the designated representative for his minor children and, pursuant to the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules), the representative is deemed to have been designated by the Division.1 II.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) allows the appeal, sets aside the determination of the RPD and refers the matter to a differently constituted panel for a re-determination taking into consideration all the evidence on the record. III. BACKGROUND A. Basis of the claims

Before the RPD, the principal appellant and his wife stated that, in their country, they did not share the political ideologies or engage in some of the illegal practices used by civil servants and military personnel with whom they had to associate in their professional lives, and that they suffered the consequences-including harassment, mistreatment and death threats-even though they did attempt to defend themselves by resorting to legal proceedings through the courts.2
In addition to their Basis of Claim Forms, the appellants submitted a number of documents as evidence before the RPD.3 B. RPD decision
The hearing before the RPD was held on August 18 and September 11, 2014, and the decision rejecting the claims for refugee protection was rendered on October 6, 2014.4
In its reasons for decision, the RPD states that the determinative issue was credibility.5

While acknowledging that the claimants' disputes with their employers regarding the conditions of employment, the labour standards and the administrative decisions made by the Venezuelan public service have been well documented,6 the RPD nevertheless found that the claimants were not credible. The RPD based its finding on a number of omissions, a contradiction regarding when they allegedly began receiving death threats, their delay in leaving the country, and their failure to claim asylum in Spain, and it did not grant probative value to a certificate of medical care and found that the principal claimant was engaging in speculation regarding the facts.7 C. Grounds of appeal and remedy sought
In their memorandum, the appellants, who were then represented by a lawyer, submit that the RPD unreasonably undermined their credibility and erred in its interpretation of the facts.8

In a detailed affidavit, the principal claimant submits that there were a number of problems during the hearing before the RPD-with their first lawyer as well as with an interpreter-that adversely affected their claims for refugee protection to the extent that they were not given the opportunity to present all their allegations.9

In their memorandum, the appellants submit that it is imperative that there be a remedy in their case because they were treated unjustly and unfairly. There are also requesting that the RAD allow their appeal, substitute the determination of the RPD and grant them the status of refugees or that of persons in need of protection.10 IV. ADMISSIBILITY OF DOCUMENTS SUBMITTED ON APPEAL A. The appellants submitted extensive documentation as part of their appeal

As of January 19, 2015,11 the appellants were no longer represented by a lawyer. Consequently, the appellants applied for an extension of time to allow them to prepare new evidence and have it translated. They also requested that new evidence be admitted as part of their appeal.12 They submitted 1,454 pages of documentation to the RAD.
I was seized with the case on May 4, 2015.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present to the RAD only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim for refugee protection or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection. It should be noted that subsection 110(4) refers to the rejection of the appellant's claim for refugee protection as the time limit, not the hearing before the RPD. After the RPD hearing, but before a decision takes effect, a party who wants to provide a document as evidence may make an application to that effect.13

In Iyamuremye, referring to the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Raza, the Federal Court states that: This case law established a legal meaning to the general application of the words "new evidence," which, in the Court's view, is consistent with Parliament's clear intention with regard to subsection 110(4) to require that the RAD review the RPD's decision as is, unless new, credible and relevant evidence arose after the rejection, that might have affected the outcome of the RPD hearing if that evidence had been presented to it.14
In Ghannadi, the Federal Court states that the factors mentioned in Raza should be considered by the RAD when analyzing whether new evidence should be admitted as part of the appeal.15

That being said, in Parminder Singh, the Federal Court notes the importance of distinguishing the role of a PRRA officer from that of a member of the RAD when interpreting subsection 110(4) of the IRPA as it relates to paragraph 113(a) of the IRPA: [51] The language of paragraph 113(a) is similar to that of subsection 110(4). The latter provision sets out that the RAD can only declare evidence admissible if it arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim or if it was not reasonably available or if the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it (unlike for paragraph 113(a), the French version of subsection 110(4) does not use "reasonably have been expected" but rather the equivalent of "normally have been expected"). The RAD however considers this evidence in a very different light than does the PRRA officer; it is doing so in an appellate review of the correctness of the RPD's determination. [52] I recognize that an appeal to the RAD is mostly intended as a "paper-based" appeal. [53] However, in considering whether to grant a hearing, the RAD may only look to admissible evidence. Given this requirement, the approach taken to applying admissibility criteria - either strictly or leniently - is of paramount importance because when a claimant, who is deserving of a hearing, is refused one, serious issues of procedural equity are potentially implicated.16

In Bahta, the Federal Court finds that the salient point for the RAD to consider when deciding whether evidence presented as part of the appeal is admissible is whether it was available or not-not whether the information it contains predates the hearing before the RPD.17

In Sow, the Federal Court reiterates its analysis that an appeal before the RAD is not the equivalent of a PRRA. The Court states that the reasons for strictly limiting the receipt of new evidence in the context of a PRRA are mostly absent from those that apply to an appeal before the RAD, particularly given the truncated timeline for completing the underlying RPD proceeding.18

I am of the opinion that, in addition to the specific criteria set out under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA that refer directly to the moment when evidence became available, or to the moment when the facts referred to took place, there are others that must also be taken into account that relate to the value of the evidence submitted, that is, its trustworthiness19 and relevance.20

Finally, the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) provide that the appeal record must contain, among other documents, a written statement indicating whether the appellant is relying on any evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, as well as a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding how that evidence meets the requirements of that subsection and how it relates to the appellant.21 C. The RAD's decision regarding the admissibility of the documents in question

The extensive documentation submitted by the appellants as part of their appeal covers various aspects of the current situation in their country of origin. At first glance, these documents appear to be useful not only to analyze their fear of persecution by reason of their political opinion, but also to analyze whether adequate protection is available from the Venezuelan authorities; this is an issue regarding which the RPD did not draw any conclusion.

That being said, in their applications, I did not find full and detailed submissions regarding how the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and how that evidence relates to them personally. I am conscious of the fact that the appellants are not represented by counsel or by a lawyer; however, in choosing to represent themselves, they are making a risky decision,22 notably that of not being completely familiar with the requirements set out under the relevant legislative provisions.
Consequently, I conclude that the evidence submitted by the appellants as part of their appeal is not admissible. V. HEARING BEFORE THE RAD A. The appellants did not request a hearing before the RAD

The RAD Rules state that the record of the person who is the subject of the appeal must include a written statement indicating whether they are requesting that a hearing be held under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, as well as a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding why the RAD should hold a hearing, if the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held.23
No request for a hearing before the RAD was found in their memorandum, in the principal appellant's detailed affidavit, or in subsequent applications made by the principal appellant and his wife.

Under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, when evidence presented on appeal is found to be admissible, it must be determined whether it raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, whether it is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and whether it would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. If so, the RAD may hold a hearing.
paragraphs.heading_before: B. Test under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA

paragraphs.text: In this case-without taking into account the fact that the appellants themselves did not request that a hearing be held before the RAD-I have found the extensive documentation submitted by the appellants as part of their appeal to be inadmissible.
paragraphs.heading_before: C. The RAD's decision on whether to hold a hearing

paragraphs.text: Consequently, I conclude that there is no cause to hold a hearing before the RAD.

In their memorandum, the appellants do not stipulate which standard of review should be applied or which approach should be taken in this appeal. Nevertheless, they do submit that a remedy should be found in their case because they were treated unjustly and unfairly.24
paragraphs.heading_before: VI. APPROACH TO BE TAKEN IN THIS APPEAL

paragraphs.text: In Djossou, Justice Martineau demonstrates that the approach then used by the RAD to determine its role compared with that of the RPD was not an acceptable outcome in law.25 He is unequivocal: an appeal before the RAD is not a judicial review, as the RAD has much broader powers on appeal than those of a court of law sitting in judicial review,26 and he urges the RAD to consider the three options before it-true appeal, appeal de novo or hybrid appeal-with an open mind.27 In the conclusion of this decision, Justice Martineau states that it does not appear appropriate to him to judicially impose any standard of deference on the RAD until such time as the Federal Court of Appeal or even the Supreme Court of Canada has decided the issue definitively. He states that, in the interim, the onus is on the RAD to review the IRPA and to adopt a new test based on an analysis that takes all the relevant factors into account. He adds that, in his opinion, the two alternative approaches (the so-called "palpable and overriding error" appellate standard of review, and the composite and variable standard of review) discussed in Alyafi are not the only options to consider-the absence of deference in the case of any error of law, fact or law and fact being also a possible option.28

I am of the opinion that procedural fairness is the determinative issue in this case. In matters of procedural fairness, no deference is owed to the RPD. It is simply a matter of determining whether procedural fairness has or has not been respected.
Taking into consideration the exceptional circumstances of this case, I conclude that procedural fairness was not respected. Here are my reasons.
paragraphs.heading_before: VII. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: Where procedural fairness is at issue, the proper approach is to ask whether the requirements of natural justice have been met in the particular circumstances of the case.29 In a claim for refugee protection before the RPD, procedural fairness ensures that the person claiming refugee protection understands the procedure, has a reasonable opportunity to tender any evidence to support their claim and has the opportunity to persuade the RPD that their claim is well founded.30 A breach of procedural fairness will not result in relief in every case. According to the case law, if it is apparent that the decision-maker would have reached the same decision notwithstanding a breach of procedural fairness, and no purpose would be achieved by referring the matter to the RPD for re-determination, the decision should stand.31

In this case, the appellants are now claiming that there were a number of problems during the hearing before the RPD, with their first lawyer as much as with the interpreter. I did not find any information on the record to establish that they filed a complaint against their former lawyer or against their interpreter and, consequently, I am of the opinion that there is no cause to blame anyone. Nevertheless, according to the appellants, these problems adversely affected their claims for refugee protection and, as a result, they were not able to present all their allegations, and they were not able to persuade the RPD that their claims for refugee protection were well founded. I am also of the opinion that the RPD should not be blamed in the circumstances, having acted as well as possible considering its constraints. Be that as it may, there can be a breach of procedural fairness even if the decision-maker did not err.32 In my opinion, in light of the particular circumstances in this case, the best way to remedy the situation is to set aside the RPD determination and hold a new hearing before a differently constituted panel of the RPD.

Even though I am of the opinion that the determination of the RPD should be set aside, I do not find that I can arrive at my own conclusions regarding whether the appellants are refugees or persons in need of protection.
paragraphs.heading_before: B. The matter should be referred to the RPD

paragraphs.text: Although the recording of the hearing in the refugee protection claims is part of the record before me, the fact remains that I cannot substitute my own determination for that of the RPD without hearing the evidence that was presented to the RPD. Moreover, my interpretation of the case law is that the credibility of the person who is the subject of the proceeding may be analyzed only within the confines of a hearing, and findings may be made in this regard only by a decision-maker who participated in the hearing and heard all the evidence.33 As part of this appeal, the appellants submitted extensive documentation regarding the overall situation in their country and, consequently, on the issue of the protection that Venezuelan authorities provide their citizens. It must be noted that the RPD did not draw any conclusion on this issue. The Federal Court has already ruled that the RAD lacks jurisdiction over issues that have not been previously decided by the RPD.34 What is certain is that the issue of whether Venezuelan authorities can provide adequate protection must be analyzed before a conclusion can be made that the appellants have a well-founded fear of persecution or that it is more likely than not that they would be personally subjected to a risk to their lives if they were to return to live in their country. Consequently, the matter must be referred to the RPD.

For these reasons, I set aside the RPD determination and refer the matter to the RPD for a re-determination by a differently constituted panel taking into account all the evidence on the record. It would undoubtedly be wise to dedicate a number of hours to this hearing to allow a full review of these claims for refugee protection.

The appeal is allowed.
